d: The sale or listing through which the fund turns an investment into cash or tradable shares. Exit planning usually starts two to three years before a sale.
x: A trade sale to a strategic buyer in year 5.
An IPO followed by staged share sales.
s: The fund holds longer, uses secondaries or partial exits.
The board weighs the offer against a full process.

d: Listing the company on a stock exchange. The fund usually sells over time after a lock-up rather than at listing.
x: A Nasdaq IPO with the fund selling 10% at listing.
An NSE listing of an Indian portfolio company.
s: Realised value is below the IPO mark.
LPs decide whether to hold or sell.

d: Period after an IPO, often 180 days, during which existing holders may not sell.
x: SEBI-mandated lock-in for certain pre-IPO shareholders.
s: Lock-up expires and many holders sell.
It waits or negotiates an early release.

d: Sale of the company to a strategic buyer, usually a larger company in the same industry. The most common exit for venture-backed companies.
x: A software startup sold to a larger software group.
A healthcare company sold to a multinational.
s: Fund receives listed stock, possibly locked up.
Part of the price depends on future performance.

d: Sale of a portfolio company to another private equity fund.
x: A mid-market fund selling to a larger buyout fund.
A third buyout of the same company.
s: It sells and buys the same asset; fees are paid twice.

d: Managers buy the business, usually backed by a PE fund and debt. Also used by funds to exit to the existing team.
x: Founders selling to management backed by a fund.
An MBO financed with vendor loan notes.
s: Price must be fair given management's information advantage.

d: Preparing an IPO and a sale at the same time, to create competition and choose the better outcome.
x: Running bankers for an IPO while sounding strategic buyers.
Dual-track ending in a trade sale at a premium.

d: A listed shell company raises cash and merges with a private company, taking it public without a traditional IPO.
x: A US SPAC merging with a fintech company.

d: Selling part of a stake, often to a new investor, to return cash while keeping upside.
x: Selling 40% of a holding to a sovereign fund.
s: Fund wants DPI before Fund II.

d: Due diligence reports commissioned by the seller and given to bidders, speeding up a sale process.
x: Financial, tax and commercial VDD in an auction.
VDD reliance letter for the winning buyer.
s: Faster process and fewer price chips.
Buyer claims against warranties or insurance.

d: The portfolio company borrows to pay a dividend to shareholders, returning cash to the fund without a sale.
x: A €50m recap returning half the fund's cost.
s: LPs check whether it came from operations or leverage.

d: An investment valued at zero or sold for nothing.
x: A startup shut down after failing to raise.

d: An LP sells its fund interest, including unfunded commitments, to a secondary buyer, usually at a discount to NAV. Transfer needs GP consent.
x: A pension selling €200m of interests at 92% of NAV.
A family office selling one tail-end interest.
s: LPAs often say consent cannot be unreasonably withheld.

d: A transaction arranged by the GP to give LPs liquidity on some assets while the GP keeps managing them, most often through a continuation vehicle.
x: A tender offer to LPs funded by a secondary buyer.
s: Independent pricing and LPAC consent needed.
ILPA guidance recommends adequate election periods.

d: A secondary buyer, arranged by the GP, offers to buy LP interests at a set price; LPs choose whether to sell. Sometimes paired with a staple.
x: Tender at 95% of NAV for all LPs.
Tender alongside the GP's new fund raise.
s: Selling LPs take a discount for liquidity.

d: A secondary purchase combined with a commitment by the buyer to the GP's new fund.
x: Buyer purchases Fund II interests and commits €50m to Fund IV.
Staple used to help a struggling raise.
s: Buyer pays a higher price because of the staple.
LPs question whether price was influenced.

d: A fund sells a slice (strip) of its interest in every portfolio company to a secondary buyer, generating liquidity while keeping exposure.
s: Strip sale returns cash across the portfolio.

d: Prices in secondary deals are quoted as a percentage of NAV. Buyout interests often trade near NAV; venture and tail-end interests at deeper discounts.
x: A buyout interest at 94% of NAV.
A VC interest at 70% of NAV.
s: Headline price is higher but present value lower.

d: Part of the secondary price paid later, often 12 months, which raises the headline price while lowering its present value.
x: Deferred consideration in an LP portfolio sale.

d: An independent adviser's view that a transaction price is fair, used in GP-led deals and related-party sales.
x: Fairness opinion on a continuation vehicle price.
Opinion for an LPAC conflict approval.
s: Opinion supports it, though LPs may want a market test too.

d: A fund that buys existing LP interests or GP-led positions, offering investors shorter duration and a reduced J-curve.
x: A $10bn secondary fund buying LP portfolios.
s: Buying at a discount boosts early returns.
Part of the return is the discount, not growth.

d: Loans made by funds directly to companies, usually mid-market and often sponsor-backed, without a bank syndicate. Floating rate, senior secured, held to maturity.
x: A €40m senior loan to a PE-backed company at Euribor + 5.5%.
A unitranche loan funding a buyout.
s: Floating-rate income rises, but borrowers' coverage falls.
Lender negotiates amendments, fees or control.

d: A single loan combining senior and subordinated debt at a blended rate, simplifying financing for the borrower.
x: Unitranche with an agreement among lenders.
s: An agreement among lenders creates first-out/last-out layers.

d: Debt with first claim on the borrower's assets and cash flows, repaid before other creditors in default.
x: First-lien term loan secured on all assets.
s: Seniority means lower risk and spread.

d: Debt ranking below senior loans, often with PIK interest or warrants, offering higher returns for higher risk.
s: Mezz holders may lose value before senior lenders.

d: Interest added to the loan principal instead of paid in cash. Preserves borrower cash but increases debt over time.
x: 4% PIK on top of cash interest.
PIK toggle allowing switch to PIK.
s: Cash income falls; credit risk rises.
Accrued PIK counted as income, but cash not yet received.

d: Promises in a loan agreement. Maintenance covenants require tests every quarter (for example leverage below 5x); incurrence covenants apply only when the borrower takes an action.
x: Net leverage covenant at 5.5x tested quarterly.
s: Lenders can demand repayment or renegotiate.
No maintenance tests; lenders act later.

d: Loans without maintenance covenants, common in broadly syndicated markets and increasingly in large private loans. Lenders lose early warning and negotiating leverage.
x: A cov-lite term loan for a large buyout.
Private loan with a springing covenant only.

d: A loan issued below par (for example at 98), giving lenders extra yield on top of interest.
s: Lender receives par, earning the discount sooner.
Both raise yield; tax treatment differs.

d: Fees or restrictions that compensate lenders if a loan is repaid early.
s: Prepayment fee due on change of control.

d: Floating-rate loans pay a base rate (SOFR, Euribor, SONIA) plus a fixed spread for credit risk.
Loan amount divided by the value of the asset or company. Lower LTV means more equity cushion.
x: 40% LTV on an enterprise value basis.

d: Debt divided by EBITDA. A key measure of credit risk and buyout financing capacity.
EBITDA (or EBIT) divided by interest expense. Shows how easily the borrower pays interest.
s: Borrower cannot pay interest from earnings.

d: Default is failure to pay or a covenant breach; recovery is the share of the loan lenders get back. Senior secured loans historically recover more than unsecured.
x: Recovery of 70% on a senior loan.
s: Defaults times loss rate reduce yield.

d: Loans secured on specific assets such as receivables, inventory, equipment or loan pools, sized by collateral value rather than cash flow.
x: Loans backed by consumer credit portfolios.
s: EU states may restrict this under AIFMD II.

d: Buying debt of companies in or near default at deep discounts, aiming to profit from recovery or by converting debt into control.
Flexible capital for complex situations: rescue financing, carve-outs, stressed companies, litigation, often mixing debt and equity.
s: Special sits fund provides capital at high cost.
SEBI has a specific Cat I sub-category for stressed assets.

d: Agreement among lenders setting ranking, enforcement rights and payment order between debt layers.
Lending to funds rather than companies: subscription lines, NAV facilities, hybrid facilities and GP financing.
s: LPs ask for disclosure of fund-level leverage.
It can call LPs directly under security.

d: Real estate and infrastructure risk bands. Core: stable, income-producing, low leverage. Core-plus: some improvement. Value-add: repositioning or lease-up. Opportunistic: development, distress, high leverage.
s: Value-add fund buys a half-empty building.
Returns depend on leasing it up.

d: Net operating income divided by property value. Lower cap rates mean higher prices. Changes in cap rates drive much real estate value change.
x: €5m NOI at a 5% cap rate implies €100m value.
Cap rates rising from 4% to 5% cut value by 20%.

d: Rental income minus property operating costs, before debt service and capital expenditure.
s: High capex assets look better on NOI.

d: Stabilised NOI divided by total project cost. Compared with market cap rates to judge development profit.
x: 7% yield on cost vs 5% market cap rate.

d: Risks from building assets: cost overruns, delays, permits, leasing. Higher returns compensate.
s: Fund finds replacement at higher cost.

d: Greenfield infrastructure is built from scratch; brownfield assets are already operating. Greenfield carries construction risk; brownfield has operating history.
x: Brownfield toll road with ten years of traffic data.

d: A government right to build or operate infrastructure and collect revenue for a fixed period, after which the asset returns to the state.
s: Value declines toward zero; returns come from cash yield.

d: Payments from a public authority for keeping an asset available, regardless of usage. Lowers demand risk.
Long-term contract where a private party finances, builds and operates public infrastructure, paid by users or the authority.
s: Contract and law protect returns to varying degrees.

d: Listed or privately placed trusts holding income-producing real estate (REIT) or infrastructure (InvIT), with high payout requirements. In India regulated by SEBI.
x: An Indian office REIT listed on NSE.
A private InvIT holding toll roads.
s: Fund exits assets into a REIT.
Yields compete with bonds; prices fall.

d: Hedge and open-ended fund equivalent of carry: a share (often 10–20%) of gains, charged periodically, usually above a high-water mark and sometimes a hurdle.
x: 20% performance fee over a high-water mark.
s: Fund gains 10% after losing 10% last year.
With a high-water mark, no fee until losses are recovered.
Investors who redeem later may pay for gains that reverse.

d: The highest NAV on which a performance fee was paid. No new fee is charged until NAV exceeds it.
x: NAV peaked at 120; fee only above 120.
s: Fund falls to 90 then rises to 115.
Manager closes a fund under water.
Investors lose HWM protection if they move.

d: The point when a performance fee becomes payable to the manager, often annually or on redemption.
Methods that make each investor pay performance fees only on their own gains, by issuing shares in series or using equalisation credits.
x: New series issued monthly, consolidated when above HWM.
s: Investor joins at a low NAV.
Series accounting tracks its own HWM.

d: A period after subscription during which investors cannot redeem (hard lock) or pay a fee to redeem (soft lock).
x: Soft lock with 3% early redemption fee.
s: Manager offers fee discount for longer lock.

d: The advance notice investors must give before redeeming from an open-ended fund.
s: Redemption rolls to the next dealing date.

d: A separate account within a fund for illiquid or hard-to-value assets, excluded from normal redemptions until realised.
x: Side pocket holding a private stake.
Side pocket created after a default.
s: It keeps its side pocket share until realised.
Often charged on cost, not value.

d: A bank providing hedge funds with financing, securities lending, custody and trade execution.
x: A fund using two prime brokers.
s: Fund must post collateral or sell.
Assets may be stuck; diversification helps.

d: Gross exposure is long plus short positions as a share of NAV; net is long minus short. Show risk and market direction.
s: Net exposure drives most of the loss.

d: Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by volatility. Higher means better return per unit of risk. Less meaningful for smoothed private market returns.
s: Fund with low returns but low volatility.

d: The largest peak-to-trough fall in NAV over a period.
